segments.text: This dynamic report uses just four Excel formulas.  No pivot tables, no macros, and it updates itself
forever. I add a new country, it's there. New  category, it's there. New orders are automatically
included, and every total recalculates. If you're  the person who rebuilds the same report every week
or every month, updating drop-downs, editing  formula ranges, you're doing hours of work that
four formulas can completely replace. Let me show  you how to build it step by step. And if you want,
you can download the free practice  file in the description or pin comment.
I'm using a sales data set for this video. There's  250 or so orders categorized by region, country,
category, product, channel, salesperson, units,  unit price, and revenue. Don't tune out if you
don't work in sales. Everything I'm about  to show you works exactly the same for any
list-based data: employees and departments,  projects and clients, invoices and vendors.
Okay, before we touch a formula, let's get  organized because how you set up a report
matters as much as the formulas inside it.  I'll start by formatting my data in an Excel
table. On the Home tab, Format as Table. And  I'm just going to use this light style here,
but you can choose something that suits  your theme or even create a custom style.
My table has headers. Click OK.  And then on the Table Design tab,
I'm just going to rename this table Sales  Data. Press Enter. And that job's done.
Now, it's a good idea to always keep your  data and your report on separate sheets. So,
in the interest of time, I've got a sheet  already set up, but you can add a new sheet
by clicking the plus icon here. I'm going to  double-click and rename this sheet Report.
Now, if we look at the completed report, you  can see it has three parts: the data sheet,
and then on the report sheet, we've  got the report itself and the workings,
or helper cells and columns. Beginners  often put everything in one place,
which gets messy. A better approach is to have  your data on its own sheet and then helper cells
on another sheet that can be hidden so the report  stays clean. But for this video, you can see I'm
breaking that rule by putting my helper cells off  to the side of my report. And this is so we can
see them while we write the formulas. Just keep in  mind that you should put them on a working sheet.
Now, the first thing we need is a list of  the countries sorted in alphabetical order.
That's going to feed our first drop-down list. And  while you could grab the countries from the data,
paste them as values, then go to the Data  tab, Remove Duplicates, I don't have a header,
so let's deselect that. Click OK. And  now I need to sort them from A to Z,
and so on and so forth. If you add  a new country to your source data,
you've got to run through all these steps  again manually, and that's way too much work.
So, let's go back to the blank file,  and I'll show you a better way. So,
I'm going to put my country list here, and I'm  going to use the UNIQUE function to reference
my Sales Data country column. And because I've  formatted my data in an Excel table, all I need
to do is hover my mouse above the column header  until it turns into the down arrow. Left-click
once and it's all selected. Press Enter, and  there's my list of distinct country names.
You can see the UNIQUE function spills the list,
and we get that blue border to show this spilled  array. And of course, because it's a formula,
if I go back to my Sales Data, let's go down  to the next row and we'll add a new country.
Let's go back to the report. You can see Italy  is now included. No more updating that formula.
Let me Ctrl+Z to get rid of Italy because  the next thing I want to do is sort this.
We can do that with the SORT function. So,  we're just wrapping the whole UNIQUE formula
in the SORT function. And now that  they're sorted in alphabetical order,
it'll just make it easier to  work with in my drop-down list.
Let's do the same for the category list.  Equals UNIQUE. We're going to reference
the category column. Hover the mouse till  it turns into the down arrow. Left-click
once. Press Enter. And don't forget, we  want to sort it. Up in the formula bar,
you can also add SORT up here. Press Enter.  And there's our sorted list of categories.
With those two jobs done, we're ready to  add our drop-down lists. The first one
is country and category. To add a drop-down  list, select the cell you want the list in.
Then on the Data tab of the ribbon, Data  Validation here, I want to allow a list,
and the source is going to be my country list  here. But instead of selecting all the cells,
I'm just going to reference the first cell in my  spilled array and then append the hash symbol.
The hash symbol tells Excel to return all the  spilled results. So I never need to update this
reference again. The list grows, the drop-down  grows. The list shrinks, the drop-down shrinks.
By the way, if you want to learn more about the  hash symbol and other important Excel symbols,
I've got a video dedicated to it, and you can  watch it by clicking the link at the top right.
Okay, let's repeat for the category  drop-down. Data Validation list. The
source is just the first cell followed  by the hash sign. Click OK, and that
job's done. Let's choose Electronics,  and for the country, we'll choose USA.
Next, we'll use the FILTER function. And  it's one of those features that changes
how you use Excel straight away, but it's just  one of many. Excel is full of small techniques
like this that save time and simplify your  work. Most people never learn them properly.
They pick up bits and pieces and stick with  slower manual ways of doing things. That's
why I created my Excel Expert course. It brings  together the most useful tools and shows you how
to use them in a logical step-by-step way,  so you're not guessing what to learn next.
Students often tell me they're working  faster, taking on more complex tasks,
and being relied on more in their roles. If  you want to build that kind of skill set,
you'll find the course linked in the description  and pinned comment. Plus, all courses are
currently 20% off until May 14, and there's a  30-day guarantee if you want to try them out.
Now, this is the main event. FILTER is the  function that does the heavy lifting in
any dynamic report. It takes two things:  the data you want back and the condition
it has to match. I'll start by grabbing the  headers from my source data because they're
going to also be used in my report and paste  them in here. Let's go and add an underline.
I'm going to use the FILTER function  to extract my Sales Data. So,
the array is my Sales Data table. Now,  to select the table, place your cursor
in the top left until it turns into the  diagonal down arrow. Left-click once,
and you can see in the formula bar it's  using the table name Sales Data. Perfect.
Comma. The next argument of FILTER, let's  just bring the tooltip up, is what you want
to include. This is my criteria, and they're  entered as logical tests. I have two criteria,
so I need to enter them inside parentheses. The  first one is where my Sales Data country equals
the country selected in my report. Close  parenthesis on that one. Then I'm going to
multiply the first criteria by the second, and  we'll come back to why we do this in a moment.
The next criteria is where the category equals  the category selected in the drop-down here.
Close parenthesis on my second criteria.  Comma. The next argument in FILTER is
what to return if no results are found. So, we  can return another formula or just some text.
I'm going to just return the text no results  found. Close parenthesis on FILTER. Press Enter.
And with that, FILTER returns the rows from the
Sales Data table that match the country  and category selected in the drop-down.
Now, to explain how this FILTER criteria  works, let's go to the Sales Data, and I'm
going to enter the formulas just beside it. So,  our first criteria was where the country equals
the country selected in the drop-down here.  Press Enter. You can see for every row it's
returning a TRUE or FALSE result. TRUE where  the country matches, FALSE where it doesn't.
And then we did the same for the category,
where the category equals the category  selected here. Press Enter. And then we
multiplied the two logical tests. And here  I'm going to use the hash to reference the
whole spilled array multiplied by the next  logical test's spilled array. Press Enter.
And now I have a series of zeros and  ones. Zero where either result was FALSE,
and one only where both results were  TRUE. And FILTER simply returns the
rows where both results are TRUE, or the logical  tests multiplied together evaluate to one. And
once you understand this technique, you can use  it in other functions like SUMPRODUCT and more.
And here's another tip. If you  ever need OR instead of AND,
simply change the multiplication to plus.  TRUE plus FALSE is one, so it keeps the row.
All right, let's delete those. We'll  go back to our report because there's
one thing that's not ideal. If I change  my country to Japan, that's all good.
Japan has Electronics. But if we change the  category to Accessories, there's no results
found. It would be better if we only give the  user the categories which Japan has available.
So, let's use the FILTER function to only return  categories in our list relevant to each country.
So, instead of just referencing the Sales Data  category, we're going to wrap it in FILTER.
We're filtering the Sales Data category where  the country equals the country selected here.
Close parenthesis on FILTER. So now we've  got three closing parentheses. Press Enter.
And now our category list only returns  Electronics for Japan. Let's choose Mexico.
Mexico has Accessories and Office. So, we  need to change Electronics here and choose
one that Mexico has. So, what we've  built here is a dependent drop-down
list. That is, the category list is  dependent on the country selected.
Now, this FILTER table is useful, but let's turn  this into a report with summary numbers at the
top. These are key facts your reader needs at  a glance before they even look at the detail.
For this report, I want to highlight  the top sales performer. So,
I need the headers Top Sales Rep, Units, and  Revenue. And let's give that an underline.
Now, for the formula, I'm going to write it  over here where I have more space so you can
see the individual steps. And then I'll  move it back up to the top of the report.
The first thing I need to do is group the  orders and sales revenue by salesperson.
And we can use the GROUPBY function to do  that. The first argument of GROUPBY is what
row fields you want to group by. I  want to group by the salesperson. So,
I'm going to use the CHOOSECOLS function  to reference my spilled array here.
So remember, we reference the spilled  array with the hash sign and return the
column the salesperson is in, which we can see  is column 7. That's the rows I want to group by.
Next, GROUPBY wants to know which  columns I want to summarize. So again,
we'll use CHOOSECOLS to reference my  spilled array here. And this time,
I want columns 8 and 10. Close  parenthesis on CHOOSECOLS.
Next, GROUPBY wants to know how I want to  aggregate these values. Well, I want to
sum them. So, I'm just going to tab to insert SUM.  Now, it wants to know if I have field headers. No,
you can see I haven't included the headers  in my range being referenced by CHOOSECOLS,
so that's zero. And do I want totals?  No, I don't need totals either. Let's
close parenthesis and press Enter  here and see what we have so far.
Now, GROUPBY returns two results, and  they're sorted in alphabetical order
based on the first column. Let's edit the  formula and make use of the next argument,
which is the sort order. Remember, I want  the top salesperson by sales revenue. So,
I want to sort by the third column in my  GROUPBY results, but I want to sort them
in descending order, so that's minus 3. Press  Enter. And now we have Sarah Chen listed first.
Now, I only want the first  row returned by GROUPBY. So,
I'm going to wrap it in the TAKE  function. So, TAKE wants the array,
that's my GROUPBY formula, and then it wants to  know which rows. Well, I only want the first row,
so that's 1. Close parenthesis on  TAKE. Press Enter. There's my results.
Let's cut this formula out, and we'll  paste it in up here. Job done. Except,
let's handle errors by wrapping our whole  formula in the IFERROR function. That way,
if we get no results here, this formula  won't return an error. We're going to
return a blank instead, denoted by  two double quotes. Close parenthesis.
And that's it. Four formulas that all work  together to dynamically build this report.
Let's go and add some new data. I'll go to  the bottom of the table. Let's copy this
record for USA because that's what our current  filters are. And I'm just going to paste it at
the bottom of the table like we've added a  new record. Let's go back. And you can see,
as you add new data, it automatically  gets included. And your users can select
items from the drop-downs to focus  in on the data that they want to see.
Now, before you go build your own, there's  three quick warnings. The first is the spill
error. If you ever see this, it means  something is blocking where your dynamic
array wants to expand. Usually, it's a  stray value in a cell below your formula.
And we can see that with the X here. Delete  whatever's in the way, and it fills back in.
Second, dynamic arrays do not play nicely  with data formatted in Excel tables. So,
let's Ctrl+T and format this in a table.  Again, we get the same spill error. I'll
Ctrl+Z to undo that. Just know that tables are  not compatible with spilled array formulas.
And lastly, most of the functions used  in this report and the hash symbol trick
only work with more modern versions of  Excel. If your functions don't appear
in the IntelliSense when you type them  in, then it's time to upgrade. Honestly,
it is worth it. You're missing a  lot more than just these functions.
Get those three things right, and this setup works  exactly the way it should. This report is just
one thing Excel can do for you automatically.  There are at least eight more you're probably
doing by hand every single week. So, click  here to keep watching. I'll see you there.
